--- title: "8. Use graphs, not tables, for model results" --- ## Why visualize model results? *"One great virtue of good graphical representation is that it can serve to display clearly and effectively a message carried by quantities whose calculation or observation is far from simple." ([Tukey and Wilk 1966](https://dl.acm.org/doi/pdf/10.1145/1464291.1464366?casa_token=i-jmHvnwKxcAAAAA:ZzNmerZ_W8OrCZA3n0N-5D-mPDAa-Ahossv9T2q41arvb26ynyVjVYhrpo4lBJzqDDALvzlYpq2ibQ))* - Visualizing data can simplify complex relationships - Visualizations often synthesize large amounts of information succinctly; relationships/patterns become clear visually - Visualizations make your data more accessible and memorable (bonus: nice visualizations make your audience less likely to fall asleep!) - *"The more visual the input becomes, the more likely it is to be recognized and recalled." ([Medina 2008](https://brainrules.net/))* ### Can you extract the sunbeams from these cucumbers? ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## Stata ```{.stata-run} . ** Ex 1: Linear Regression with Interaction . use "https://tdmize.github.io/data/data/dmv_intsim01.dta", clear . . qui regress y b c . estimates store mod1a . . qui regress y c.c##i.b . estimates store mod1b . . qui regress y c.c##i.b x1 . estimates store mod1c . . esttab mod1a mod1b mod1c, noomit nobase se /// > title("Linear interaction models") Linear interaction models ------------------------------------------------------------ (1) (2) (3) y y y ------------------------------------------------------------ b 4.600 (3.657) c -0.537*** -0.978*** -0.978*** (0.0465) (0.0629) (0.0629) 1.b 3.107 3.199 (3.571) (3.574) 1.b#c.c 0.920*** 0.920*** (0.0908) (0.0908) x1 -1.204 (1.786) _cons 28.19*** 28.86*** 28.81*** (2.587) (2.525) (2.526) ------------------------------------------------------------ N 2000 2000 2000 ------------------------------------------------------------ Standard errors in parentheses * p<0.05, ** p<0.01, *** p<0.001 ``` ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(foreign) # load Stata datasets library(ggplot2) # main graphics package library(dplyr) # data manipulation tools library(marginaleffects) # predictions and marginal effects library(modelsummary) # coefficient plots & nice tables library(cleanplots) # Mize's graphics scheme ## Use cleanplots colors, markers, lines, and theme for all graphs ## cleanplots_defaults() theme_update(plot.title.position = "plot") # titles start at left edge of graph # Simulated data for interaction exs intsim01 <- read.dta("https://tdmize.github.io/data/data/dmv_intsim01.dta") # b is a binary (0/1) group variable intsim01$b <- factor(intsim01$b) ## Ex 1: Linear Regression with Interaction ## mod1a <- lm(y ~ b + c, data = intsim01) mod1b <- lm(y ~ b * c, data = intsim01) mod1c <- lm(y ~ b * c + x1, data = intsim01) modelsummary(list(mod1a, mod1b, mod1c), stars = TRUE) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}

(3) Is the effect of *c* (when *b* = 1) positive or negative? (4) Where across the range of *c* is the difference between *b* = 0 and *b* = 1 statistically significant? (5) Where is the observed data? ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## Stata ```{.stata-run} . // 8.a - Plot the predictions . estimates restore mod1c (results mod1c are active now) . qui margins, at(c=(-150(5)150) b=(0 1)) . . *Generate variables to make rugs on plot . gen pipe = "|" if c != . // What rug looks like . gen where = -150 // Where on y-axis to put rug . . marginsplot, /// > recastci(rline) ciopt(lpat(dash) col(gs12)) plotopt(msym(none)) /// > addplot(scatter where c, ms(none) mlabel(pipe) mlabcol(gs6) /// > xlab(-150(50)150) ylab(-150(50)150) xline(0) yline(0) legend(order(3 "b=0" > 4 "b=1"))) /// > title("[8.a] Predictions from linear regression that includes b*c product > term") /// > ytitle("Predicted y") xtitle("c") Variables that uniquely identify margins: c b ``` ![](fig/dmv-08_a-preds_int_linear.png){width=80% fig-alt="[8.a] Predicted y across c from -150 to 150 for b = 0 and b = 1, with 95% confidence intervals and a rug of the observed c values along the bottom: for b = 0 the prediction falls steeply from about 175 to about -120, for b = 1 it is nearly flat around 30, and the lines cross near c = 0."} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # 8.a - Plot the predictions plot_predictions(mod1c, condition = c("c", "b")) + geom_rug(data = intsim01, mapping = aes(x = c), sides = "b", alpha = 0.3, inherit.aes = FALSE) + geom_hline(yintercept = 0) + labs(x = "c", y = "Predicted y", color = "b", fill = "b", title = "[8.a] Predictions from linear regression that includes b*c product term") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](8-model-results_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-2-1.png){fig-alt='[8.a] Predicted y across c for b = 0 and b = 1, with 95% confidence intervals and a rug of the observed c values along the bottom: for b = 0 the prediction falls steeply, for b = 1 it is nearly flat, and the lines cross near c = 0.' width=80%} ::: ::: ::: ### Can you extract the sunbeams from these cucumbers? ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## Stata ```{.stata-run} . ** Ex 2: Binary Logit with Interaction . use "https://tdmize.github.io/data/data/dmv_intsim02.dta", clear . . qui logit y b c . estimates store mod2a . . qui logit y c.c##i.b . estimates store mod2b . . qui logit y c.c##i.b x1 . estimates store mod2c . . esttab mod2a mod2b mod2c, noomit nobase se /// > title("Logit interaction models") Logit interaction models ------------------------------------------------------------ (1) (2) (3) y y y ------------------------------------------------------------ y b -4.225*** (0.262) c 0.487*** 0.147 0.148 (0.0832) (0.313) (0.313) 1.b -6.363** -6.366** (1.950) (1.950) 1.b#c.c 0.366 0.367 (0.325) (0.325) x1 -0.0575 (0.0622) _cons 1.257* 3.238 3.235 (0.539) (1.877) (1.877) ------------------------------------------------------------ N 2000 2000 2000 ------------------------------------------------------------ Standard errors in parentheses * p<0.05, ** p<0.01, *** p<0.001 ``` ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Simulated data for interaction exs intsim02 <- read.dta("https://tdmize.github.io/data/data/dmv_intsim02.dta") intsim02$b <- factor(intsim02$b) ## Ex 2: Binary Logit with Interaction ## mod2a <- glm(y ~ b + c, family = binomial, data = intsim02) mod2b <- glm(y ~ b * c, family = binomial, data = intsim02) mod2c <- glm(y ~ b * c + x1, family = binomial, data = intsim02) modelsummary(list(mod2a, mod2b, mod2c), stars = TRUE) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}

(3) Is the effect of *c* (when *b* = 1) positive or negative? (4) Where across the range of *c* is the difference between *b* = 0 and *b* = 1 statistically significant? (5) Where is the observed data? ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## Stata ```{.stata-run} . // 8.b - Plot the predictions . estimates restore mod2c (results mod2c are active now) . qui margins, at(c=(3(.25)9) b=(0 1)) . . *Generate variables to make rugs on plot . gen pipe = "|" if c != . // What rug looks like . gen where = 0 // Where on y-axis to put rug . . marginsplot, /// > recastci(rline) ciopt(lpat(dash) col(gs12)) plotopt(msym(none)) /// > addplot(scatter where c, ms(none) mlabel(pipe) mlabcol(gs6) /// > xlab(3(1)9) ylab(0(.2)1) legend(order(3 "b=0" 4 "b=1"))) /// > title("[8.b] Predictions from binary logit model that includes b*c product > term") /// > ytitle("Predicted probability") xtitle("c") Variables that uniquely identify margins: c b ``` ![](fig/dmv-08_b-preds_int_logit.png){width=80% fig-alt="[8.b] Predicted probabilities across c from 3 to 9 for b = 0 and b = 1, with 95% confidence intervals and a rug of the observed c values: for b = 0 the probability is flat near 1, while for b = 1 it rises steadily from about .17 to about .82."} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # 8.b - Plot the predictions plot_predictions(mod2c, condition = c("c", "b"), rug = TRUE) + labs(x = "c", y = "Predicted probability", color = "b", fill = "b", title = "[8.b] Predictions from binary logit model that includes b*c product term") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](8-model-results_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-4-1.png){fig-alt='[8.b] Predicted probabilities across c for b = 0 and b = 1, with 95% confidence intervals and a rug of the observed c values: for b = 0 the probability is flat near 1, while for b = 1 it rises steadily.' width=80%} ::: ::: ::: \*Curious how this is possible? See [Mize 2019](https://sociologicalscience.com/articles-v6-4-81/) on nonlinear interaction effects ### Giant regression tables in talks = ☹ ```{.stata-output} [11.0] Linear Regression Results - Log Hourly Wages ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- (1) (2) (3) ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Woman R -0.37*** (0.01) -0.37*** (0.01) -0.36*** (0.01) high school 0.36*** (0.01) 0.35*** (0.01) junior college 0.57*** (0.02) 0.56*** (0.02) bachelor 0.78*** (0.02) 0.76*** (0.02) graduate 1.02*** (0.02) 0.98*** (0.02) black -0.08*** (0.01) -0.03* (0.01) other -0.05** (0.02) -0.07*** (0.02) age of respondent 0.01*** (0.00) 0.01*** (0.00) Currently Married 0.15*** (0.01) Number of Children -0.00 (0.00) catholic 0.05*** (0.01) jewish 0.17*** (0.03) none 0.01 (0.01) other 0.01 (0.03) buddhism 0.06 (0.07) hinduism 0.25* (0.10) other eastern 0.38* (0.17) moslem/islam -0.29** (0.10) orthodox-christian 0.07 (0.10) christian -0.01 (0.04) native american 0.01 (0.20) inter-nondenominat~l -0.05 (0.08) Lives in Metro Area 0.05*** (0.01) Midwest -0.09*** (0.01) South -0.13*** (0.01) West -0.04** (0.01) Constant 2.65*** (0.01) 1.61*** (0.02) 1.61*** (0.02) ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Observations 31102 31021 30876 ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Standard errors in parentheses * p<0.05, ** p<0.01, *** p<0.001 ``` ![](images/just-say-no.jpeg){width=30% fig-alt="Nancy Reagan speaking at a podium with a sign that reads Just say no."} ## Coefficient plots - Coefficient plots are very effective for replacing regression tables (of coefficients) in talks and (sometimes) in articles/reports - Coefficient plots also display multiple model results better than tables--- making it easy to compare estimates across models - Measures of uncertainty (e.g., CIs) are also easily incorporated and visually easily processed :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="70%"} ![](images/petts-mize-kaufman-2022.png){fig-alt="Published coefficient plot: effects of experimental conditions on commitment penalty, with separate estimates and confidence intervals for mothers and fathers."} ::: ::: {.column width="30%"} ::: {.callout-note icon="false" appearance="simple"} Figure 1 from [Petts, Mize, and Kaufman 2022](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1jx7l6Rl9AbR4_YRxJZPwqWG-F0Ti1lgJ/view?usp=sharing) ::: ::: :::: ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## Stata ```{.stata-run} . use "https://tdmize.github.io/data/data/addhealth4.dta", clear (addhealth4_dmv.dta | Add Health Wave IV | DMV Workshop) . . // 8.c - Coefficients from a linear regression model . qui regress subjclass i.woman i.race3 c.age c.income i.college i.workstat . . coefplot, xline(0) xlab(-1(.5)1) baselevels ciop(col(gs12)) drop(_cons 0.woman > ) /// > title("[8.c] Predictors of Subjective Class Standing - Linear Regression") > /// > note("Effects above zero indicate higher subjective class standing") ``` ![](fig/dmv-08_c-coefplot.png){width=80% fig-alt="[8.c] Coefficient plot of predictors of subjective class standing with 95% confidence intervals and a dashed line at zero: having a college degree has by far the largest effect (about 0.94), women are slightly higher (about 0.15), and the other effects are near zero."} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Add Health Wave 4 Data ah4 <- droplevels(read.dta("https://tdmize.github.io/data/data/addhealth4.dta")) # Subjective class standing is a 1 to 10 scale ah4$subjclass <- as.numeric(ah4$subjclass) # 8.c - Coefficients from a linear regression model reg_sc <- lm(subjclass ~ woman + race3 + age + income + college + workstat, data = ah4) modelplot(reg_sc, coef_omit = "Intercept") + geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "gray20") + scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(-1, 1.5, .5)) + scale_y_discrete(limits = rev) + labs(title = "[8.c] Predictors of Subjective Class Standing - Linear Regression", caption = "Effects above zero indicate higher subjective class standing") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](8-model-results_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-5-1.png){fig-alt='[8.c] Coefficient plot of predictors of subjective class standing with 95% confidence intervals and a dashed line at zero: having a college degree has by far the largest effect, women are slightly higher, and the other effects are near zero.' width=80%} ::: ::: ::: ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## Stata ```{.stata-run} . // 8.d - Separate models for men and women . qui regress subjclass i.race3 c.age c.income i.college i.workstat if woman == > 0 . est store scmen . . qui regress subjclass i.race3 c.age c.income i.college i.workstat if woman == > 1 . est store scwom . . coefplot (scmen, label("Men")) (scwom, label("Women")), /// > xline(0) xlab(-1(.5)1) baselevels ciop(col(*.5)) drop(*_cons) /// > title("[8.d] Predictors of Subjective Class Standing - Linear Regression") > /// > subtitle("Separate Models for Men and Women") /// > note("Effects above zero indicate higher subjective class standing") ``` ![](fig/dmv-08_d-coefplot_by_gender.png){width=80% fig-alt="[8.d] Coefficient plot with separate estimates for men (red) and women (light blue) side by side for each predictor: the college degree effect is large for both (about 1.04 for men and 0.90 for women), and the other effects are small for both."} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # 8.d - Fit separate models for men and women reg_men <- lm(subjclass ~ race3 + age + income + college + workstat, data = subset(ah4, woman == "Man")) reg_wom <- lm(subjclass ~ race3 + age + income + college + workstat, data = subset(ah4, woman == "Woman")) mp_gender <- modelplot(list("Men" = reg_men, "Women" = reg_wom), coef_omit = "Intercept", draw = FALSE) ggplot(mp_gender, aes(x = estimate, y = term, color = model)) + geom_linerange(aes(xmin = conf.low, xmax = conf.high), alpha = .5, position = position_dodge(width = .5)) + geom_point(size = 2.5, position = position_dodge(width = .5)) + geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "gray20") + scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(-1, 1.5, .5)) + scale_y_discrete(limits = rev) + labs(x = "Coefficient estimates and 95% confidence intervals", y = "", color = "", title = "[8.d] Predictors of Subjective Class Standing - Linear Regression", subtitle = "Separate Models for Men and Women", caption = "Effects above zero indicate higher subjective class standing") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](8-model-results_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-6-1.png){fig-alt='[8.d] Coefficient plot with separate estimates for men and women side by side for each predictor: the college degree effect is large for both, and the other effects are small for both.' width=80%} ::: ::: ::: ### Published example ![](images/hainmueller-2015.png){width=80% fig-alt="Published figure: coefficient plots of the effects of immigrant attributes on the probability of being preferred for admission, one panel for each survey design."} Figure 1 from [Hainmueller, Hangartner, and Yamamoto 2015](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1416587112) ### Coefficient plots: not just for coefficients - Increasingly, most health and social science fields are moving towards reporting marginal effects for categorical models instead of coefficients - A "coefficient plot" can be used to plot any effect ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## Stata ```{.stata-run} . use "https://tdmize.github.io/data/data/pew16.dta", clear (pew16_dmv.dta | Pew 2016 Pre-Election Data | DMV Workshop) . . qui logit trump i.woman c.age ib4.educ i.religB c.income ib3.region, or . . * Average marginal effects (AMEs) for all predictors . margins, dydx(*) post Average marginal effects Number of obs = 1,604 Model VCE: OIM Expression: Pr(trump), predict() dy/dx wrt: 1.woman age 1.educ 2.educ 3.educ 5.educ 1.religB income 1.region 2.region 4.region ------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | Delta-method | dy/dx std. err. z P>|z| [95% conf. interval] --------------+---------------------------------------------------------------- woman | Woman | -0.135 0.024 -5.742 0.000 -0.181 -0.089 age | 0.002 0.001 3.576 0.000 0.001 0.004 | educ | Less than HS | -0.197 0.066 -2.981 0.003 -0.326 -0.067 HS Degree | 0.141 0.036 3.978 0.000 0.072 0.211 Some College | 0.062 0.032 1.931 0.053 -0.001 0.126 Graduate D.. | -0.165 0.032 -5.176 0.000 -0.228 -0.103 | religB | Religious | 0.193 0.024 8.121 0.000 0.146 0.240 income | 0.000 0.000 1.761 0.078 -0.000 0.001 | region | Northeast | -0.111 0.033 -3.335 0.001 -0.176 -0.046 Midwest | -0.012 0.032 -0.379 0.705 -0.074 0.050 West | -0.093 0.032 -2.926 0.003 -0.155 -0.031 ------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Note: dy/dx for factor levels is the discrete change from the base level. . est store ames . . // 8.e - Coefficient plot of the AMEs . coefplot ames, xline(0) xlab(-.4(.1).4) ciop(col(gs12)) /// > baselevels drop(0.woman 0.religB) /// > title("[8.e] Binary Logit: Average Marginal Effects of Support for Trump v > s Clinton") /// > note("Effects above zero indicate more support for Trump") ``` ![](fig/dmv-08_e-ames.png){width=80% fig-alt="[8.e] Plot of the average marginal effects on support for Trump vs Clinton with 95% confidence intervals: being religious (about .19) and having a high school degree (about .14) increase support, while being a woman (about -.14), having less than high school (about -.20) or a graduate degree (about -.17), and living in the Northeast or West decrease it."} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Pew 2016 election data pew <- droplevels(read.dta("https://tdmize.github.io/data/data/pew16.dta")) # Bachelor's degree and the South as reference groups (as in Stata ex) pew$educ <- relevel(pew$educ, ref = "Bachelors Degree") pew$region <- relevel(pew$region, ref = "South") logit_trump <- glm(trump ~ woman + age + educ + religB + income + region, family = binomial, data = pew) # Average marginal effects (AMEs) for all predictors ames <- avg_slopes(logit_trump) ames ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` r-output Term Contrast Estimate Std.
